instance_type: One S3-class object-store prefix/partition (single partitioned key prefix), GET/HEAD read requests, sustained steady-state after auto-partition warmup. Anchored on AWS S3 us-east-1; corroborated by Google Cloud Storage per-bucket read threshold.
workload_shape: Sustained (not burst) read request rate against a SINGLE prefix/partition: GET/HEAD object reads, small-object key-value style access. Steady-state operating point after S3 has finished gradual background auto-scaling — a fast spike to this rate before warmup yields 503 (Slow Down) errors. Excludes the cross-prefix aggregate (scaling out across N prefixes multiplies this: e.g. 10 prefixes ~ 55,000 reads/s) and excludes large-object byte throughput (a separate Gb/s metric).
config_notes: PER-UNIT MEANING: this is the sustained request rate ONE prefix/partition of an S3-class object store serves for GET/HEAD reads — the natural per_instance_rps unit for an object_store component, where the "instance" = one partitioned key prefix, NOT the whole bucket/service. SERVICE LIMIT vs HARDWARE CAPACITY: this is a soft per-partition service floor, not a hard cap — AWS phrases it as "at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE or 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix," so 5,500 is a documented guaranteed-minimum for reads, with writes at the lower 3,500/s (model writes separately). REGIME: sustained steady-state, NOT instantaneous — S3 auto-scales a prefix GRADUALLY (background partitioning can take ~30-60 min); driving a cold prefix to 5,500/s immediately returns 503 Slow Down until warm. SCALES ACROSS PREFIXES: "There are no limits to the number of prefixes in a bucket," so bucket-level capacity = (per-prefix rate) x (number of well-distributed prefixes); AWS cites 10 prefixes -> 55,000 reads/s, GCS cites a 1-char random hex prefix scaling to ~80,000 reads/s. So this datapoint models ONE unit; multiply by prefix-fanout for aggregate object-store throughput, never use 5,500 as a whole-service ceiling. BAND HONESTY: central 5,500 = AWS GET/HEAD per-prefix figure; low 4,800 absorbs GCS's independent comparable "no ramp-up below 5000 read requests per second" threshold and the "at least"/warmup reality; high 6,500 gives modest headroom above the guaranteed minimum without claiming the multi-prefix aggregate. Relative half-width ~15%, clearing the T1 >=10% floor; wider than a single-vendor read because the two vendor anchors (AWS 5,500 / GCS 5,000) genuinely differ. EXCLUSIONS: PUT/write rate (3,500/s, lower), large-object Gb/s throughput, S3 Express One Zone / directory buckets (higher-perf class), and cross-prefix aggregates.

There are no limits to the number of prefixes in a bucket. ... if you create 10 prefixes in an Amazon S3 bucket to parallelize reads, you could scale your read performance to 55,000 read requests per second." Also verbatim: "While Amazon S3 is scaling to your new higher request rate, you may see some 503 (Slow Down) errors." Conditions: sustained per-prefix GET/HEAD reads, steady-state after gradual auto-scaling.

citations.note: Verbatim figures on the page: GET/HEAD "5,500 requests per second to retrieve data"; PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE "3,500 requests per second to add data"; and "There are no limits to the number of prefixes." Conditions: per-prefix request rate; introduced the current per-prefix model.

instance_type: Amazon S3 Standard, small-object GET, accessed from an EC2 client in the same AWS Region (single request, no parallelization, no CDN/cache)
workload_shape: Single small-object (<~512 KB to a few MB) GET, measuring time-to-first-byte (TTFB) per request — not aggregate throughput and not full-object transfer time. Steady-state in-region access (not cold-start, not cross-region).
config_notes: This is FIRST-BYTE (TTFB) latency for ONE object-store GET unit, NOT full-object transfer time (full transfer adds bytes/bandwidth-dependent time on top — keep them separate in the model). Two regimes appear in the evidence: (1) in-region EC2->S3 independent benchmarks cluster the median/p90 first byte at ~20-30 ms (dvassallo: p90 ~20 ms; Quickwit: typically up to 30 ms; DoltHub production round-trip ~30 ms) — value=30 ms reflects this corroborated central case; (2) AWS's own conservative envelope quotes 'roughly 100-200 ms' for small-object/first-byte-out latencies, which bundles less-optimal network paths and is a service-guidance ceiling, not a hardware floor. Tail latency is materially worse than the median: Quickwit notes '80ms is rather common', so the band high (80) captures the common p99-ish tail of the in-region regime rather than fake-tightening to the median. The band is intentionally wide (20->80, half-width ~100% of value) because real-world TTFB spans config/network/percentile heavily; it does NOT extend to AWS's full 200 ms ceiling because that figure mixes in cross-path/cross-region cases outside the in-region single-GET regime modeled here. EXCLUDES: S3 Express One Zone (single-digit ms, different storage class), CloudFront/ElastiCache caching (single-digit ms), Transfer Acceleration, multi-prefix/parallel aggregate throughput, and cross-region access. This is a typical-config latency, not a service-limit/SLA guarantee (S3 publishes no latency SLA).

instance_type: Managed/self-hosted API gateway, single region, basic proxy path (no heavy auth/transform); measured as the gateway's OWN added latency = total Latency minus backend IntegrationLatency
workload_shape: Sustained per-request proxy load near each product's reference operating point (Kong: K6 load test, basic proxy; APISIX: typical 3-plugin config). This is a PER-REQUEST added-latency overhead, NOT a throughput/capacity limit.
config_notes: PER-UNIT MEANING: ms of latency the gateway ITSELF adds per request — the AWS-canonical "service overhead" = Latency - IntegrationLatency (gateway receives→returns, minus backend time). It is NOT backend/Lambda execution time and NOT a service-LIMIT or hardware-capacity figure (it is an added-latency overhead, unlike rps which is often an account/service rate limit). REGIME: steady-state proxying; tail latency (p99) sits above the median, so central 5ms reflects a realistic p95-ish overhead, not best-case median. Central 5ms ~ Kong v3.14 basic-proxy p99 5.24ms (no plugins) measured with K6, which is effectively pure gateway latency. BAND [1,20]: floor 1ms = well-optimized NGINX/LuaJIT-class proxies and DB-less Kong (lucaberton 2026: Envoy <1ms, DB-less Kong/Traefik ~2ms; APISIX 1-2ms with typical plugins); ceiling 20ms absorbs AWS-managed API Gateway service overhead and plugin/auth-heavy configs (auth checks, request/response transforms, logging, WAF, TLS each add ms; AWS resource-based-vs-role IAM alone is a documented 10-30ms swing). EXCLUSIONS: backend/integration time, cold-start, network RTT to the client, and OAuth token-introspection (50-100ms external calls) are out of scope — those are not the gateway's base processing overhead. Band relative half-width ~190%, far above the T2 15% floor; intentionally WIDE because real-world overhead genuinely spans sub-1ms (Envoy/APISIX) to tens of ms (managed gateway + auth), and tightening would be dishonest. Vendor benchmarks (Kong) are first-party load tests, so T2 not T1.

The latency includes the integration latency and other API Gateway overhead.' and 'IntegrationLatency | The time between when API Gateway relays a request to the backend and when it receives a response from the backend.' instance_type: managed_api_gateway_account_throttle
workload_shape: Steady-state synchronous request traffic hitting a managed API gateway's default per-account/per-Region throttle quota; the 429 ("Too Many Requests") ceiling a single deployment encounters before requesting a quota raise. Mixed light request/response payloads, no per-route usage-plan override applied. Not a hardware saturation point.
config_notes: Managed-gateway DEFAULT ACCOUNT/SERVICE THROTTLE QUOTA — the 429 rate-limit ceiling a deployment hits, analogous to a payment-gateway rate limit. A SOFT, RAISABLE service limit set by the provider, NOT hardware/instance capacity. ANCHORING: AWS API Gateway is the sole genuine SAME-KIND anchor (a default account/Region throttle quota), documenting BOTH a 10,000 rps default (major Regions) and a 2,500 rps default (13 smaller Regions), explicitly adjustable ("Can be increased: Yes") — these two AWS figures define the band spread. Azure API Management and GCP API Gateway corroborate the KIND (managed gateways ship a default, raisable service-rate limit) but are NOT same-kind rps quota anchors: Azure's per-unit figure is an "estimated maximum throughput for capacity planning" (a soft capacity estimate, explicitly not a call limit), and GCP's default is in quota-units/100s (a different unit). Central 5,000 rps sits STRICTLY INSIDE [2,500, 12,000] (not at either edge). FLOOR 2,500 = AWS's own documented low default; CEILING 12,000 = a reasoned raisable-headroom ASSUMPTION above the 10,000 major-region default (not a documented figure). EXCLUDES per-route usage-plan / Apigee SpikeArrest policy ceilings (a different kind) and single-instance hardware throughput. Tier T2: rests on ONE same-kind vendor (AWS) plus cross-vendor KIND corroboration, not two independent same-kind measurements. Half-width ~95% of central, far above the T2 >=15% floor.

instance_type: PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB READ REPLICA, sysbench oltp_point_select warm-cache single-row primary-key point SELECT (server-side execution), ~4 vCPU / 8-16 GB, default config
config_notes: UNIT = server-side execution latency of ONE warm-cache single-row indexed point read (one row fetched by primary key) on a read REPLICA — the same engine-side indexed lookup a point query runs on the primary, since a replica serves identical read SQL. REGIME = warm/sustained (dataset/index resident in buffer pool/shared_buffers), default config, low-moderate concurrency (1-16 threads). EXCLUDES, by design: replication lag (the apply/visibility delay before a written row is readable on the replica), client-to-replica network RTT, connection-pool/driver overhead, queueing, and cold-cache disk fetch — those are what actually push real-world replica read latency to ms/tens-of-ms, NOT the indexed lookup itself. This is SERVER-SIDE, not end-to-end. Evidence: two independent single-node PG/MySQL sysbench oltp_point_select benchmarks cluster server-side execution at ~0.14-0.32 ms (DoltHub: PG 15.5 0.14 ms / MySQL 8.0.35 0.18 ms MEDIAN, m5a.xlarge 4 vCPU/16 GB default config; computingforgeeks: PG 0.22 / MariaDB 0.25 / MySQL 0.32 ms AVG, 4 vCPU/8 GB/16 threads/2 GB buffer pool warm). A third independent org (PingCAP/TiDB) reports oltp_point_select avg 0.28 ms / 95th-pct 0.38 ms, corroborating the sub-ms regime and the tail — but it is a DISTRIBUTED SQL engine (extra coordination hop), so it is used only as supporting corroboration, NOT to set the central value. Central 0.3 ms is deliberately CONSERVATIVE: it leans toward the slower MySQL/MariaDB AVG end (0.32/0.25) rather than the fastest DoltHub median (0.14), so it does not cherry-pick a headline. Band [0.15, 0.7]: low = fastest stated median (DoltHub PG 0.14, rounded to 0.15); high = slower-engine avg (0.32) plus the observed p95 tail (~0.38) and a modest concurrency margin, WITHOUT importing any tool/round-trip overhead. Central 0.3 sits INSIDE the band (not at an edge); relative half-width ~92%, far above the T2 15% floor — intentionally wide because the real evidence genuinely spans engines (PG fastest -> MySQL slowest) and configs, and tightening would be dishonest. Mirrors the already-grounded sql_db point-select datapoint (value 0.3) by design: a replica's server-side point read IS the same lookup as the primary's. T2 (synthetic load tests, not vendor datasheet).

instance_type: stripe
config_notes: SERVICE LIMIT, not hardware capacity. This is Stripe's published global API rate limit = the sustained request rate ONE Stripe account may drive against the API, measured in API requests per second, PER STRIPE ACCOUNT (a quota the integrator must stay under), not a measure of Stripe's underlying throughput. Central 100 = the DOCUMENTED DEFAULT for LIVE mode (test/sandbox mode is lower at 25 rps — out of scope for this live-mode datapoint). NO separate read-vs-write requests-per-second limits are published: the global rps limit applies to all API requests equally. Stripe does separately expose an "API read request allocation" (a 30-day rolling allocation of read calls, NOT a per-second cap) and states "Write API requests have no allocation limit" — but that allocation is a different mechanism and is NOT this rps figure. RAISABLE / per-account: the limit is not a hard ceiling — Stripe instructs accounts expecting a spike to "contact Stripe Support," and increases are granted on request (documented precedent: the usage-reporting endpoint is raisable from 100 to 200 rps per account on request); hence the band high (200) reflects a documented raised ceiling while the central holds the documented default. Band is widened above the T1 10% floor specifically to honestly span the raisable ceiling; low (85) reflects practical sub-default burst/headroom variance. EXCLUDED: test/sandbox 25 rps; the separate read-allocation quota; any negotiated enterprise ceiling beyond 200. measured_date 2026-06-30.
